And until the cross comes on, I'm not sure which names Defence may seek to elicit. So in this specification, we do not wish the name of this person to go on the record for personal security of this individual. And again, we would propose to proceed by way of having the name put in writing and then kept under seal, if the Chamber indeed want the name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: This whole A/B hearing and rescheduling and all this stuff, we wouldn't even be here -- we wouldn't even have to do this maybe if we'd been given all the witness statements in the chain of custody with respect to PID 3. That's all we asked for. And we were told or given through a witness statement of Mr. O'Donnell that he talked to all these witnesses and he had evidence on the chain of custody. But that's all. We didn't have any information on what the witnesses were going to say, which is the most important thing. Who cares what their names are. That was the whole point of even objecting. We could have saved a lot of court time and we can still save court time if, as the law requires in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, we know all the circumstances regarding the seizure of the document. The whole test of whether or not it's admissible and authenticated is reliability and probative value. If we don't have any of the information -- I mean, this is just taking so much time, when we probably could have settled this out of court if they would just give us the information. We've been given no notice as to what happened when this document was seized. We were told -- I hear -- well, it was in his witness statement that this document was seized in 1992 and that he saw it for the first time in 1997 when he obtained it in Sarajevo. What happened between 1992 and 1997? What happened in 1992? Was there a search warrant? You know, AID -- I mean, that's the whole point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: We have spent so much time going round and round and taking the Court's time and taking all of our valuable time when if we could just get the chain of custody of this one document -- we don't even need to talk about these other versions of this document. That's the whole point, Your Honour, that we've been trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I mind my colleagues desire not to waste Court time on this; however, as I think our submissions have shown, we have spent numerous time trying to provide information, evidence, to the Defence. We've been available at all cases as to questions going to the admissibility of this document. It eventually came to this hearing. The Chamber may be aware that this case -- this document also got called in to question in the case of Talic. In fact, all our documentation was used for that case. Mr. O'Donnell was prepared to testify, when the Defence seeing the documentation withdrew their objection. Now, it is of course the prerogative of this Defence not to follow that line. But I think that Ms. Baen is adopting here a very specific particular common law approach to this evidentiary hearing which is maybe more common to her own jurisdiction, which I with full respect do not completely agree is appropriate in this jurisdiction. This question as to admissibility of this document, which is what this hearing was about, was addressed at some length by the Trial Chamber in Talic and Brdjanin on the 28th of January and lots of the jurisprudence from the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal was discussed by the Trial Chamber in that decision. And so the question is whether or not a document should be admissible then is to the general reliability of the document, including the general circumstances of its seizure. Now, Mr. O'Donnell has come here to testify on that and testified to certain knowledge. It doesn't require in my -- in our submission, the disclosure of every single chain of custody document for every single document which the OTP has. That hasn't been the practice to date. And the testimony is -- from Mr. O'Donnell, it's his credibility as to whether he spoke to these people and the information he received. And unless we're being challenged to call every individual who may at one time have seized a document during the war period or since or handle it, I think the burden on this Tribunal will be in the extreme. So it's my submission that Mr. O'Donnell can provide information but the submissions that Ms. Baen has made as to the waste of time to the Court by showing the other documents and by not having the chain of custody statements is misplaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I think the best way to go about this is simply to allow Ms. Baen to cross-examine and see what information she wants to seek from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And if any questions are misplaced, of course the Bench will say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Baen, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I would like to apologise to Ms. Reidy. I did not -- she's worked very well with us. And I -- if she was offended by me saying she wasted time, I did not mean to offend her. Secondly, with respect to what she mentioned about Brdjanin and Talic, that case, the lawyer on that case has been here - he's a Defence lawyer. He's here for four years - is a very good friend of mine, and we've discussed this document at length. He's actually the person who recruited me over here in this Tribunal. The reason why -- if she wants to talk about the reason why he said to let it in is because there's no way they can ever bring the author of this document to authenticate the document. You can let it all in, but the jurisprudence of the Tribunal says if you cannot produce the author of the document, then it is not authenticated and should be given no weight. That goes all the way back to the Tadic hearsay decision in two separate decisions by the Trial Chamber in Celebici. That is why -- they said go ahead and just let it in this other case, just so this Trial Chamber is aware of what's going on in the other Trial Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So proceed with your questions, Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I don't even know where I left off. Okay. The document is here now, PID 3? Did it arrive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it available or not yet available? MR. DI FAZIO: It's here and the accompanying rubber gloves to handle it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Can we please see the document? Can the Trial Chamber see it?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: May I suggest that the document is -- I think it is visible is in a plastic bag and is currently under seal. And it's Mr. O'Donnell who sealed it, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I was wondering. Because if it's visible from the plastic seal, then this Defence counsel can look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: No. Within the plastic seal, it is again in an envelope which has been sealed, and it is under that seal which Mr. O'Donnell has placed his signature as the last person to have opened it. So if the Bench and the Defence counsel would like to inspect the folder and then maybe Mr. O'Donnell could break the seal and the document inside it could also be available for inspection.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour. We've already seen it and we know what it looks like. But we would like for the Trial Chamber to be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But for purposes of your cross-examination, you can go ahead without looking at it. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Judge Singh has asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. But for your continuation of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Well, my first question when I got up here, I was going to ask him if he had this "original" here with him, and I was going to ask him to let the Trial Chamber see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can see it at our own time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Well, my cross-examination -- I'll try to work with the Chamber. My cross-examination was going to follow, which I thought was the most important thing, was the viewing of the actual document. But if you want to look at it later, then I respect the Court's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go ahead with your cross-examination. In the meantime, the Trial Chamber can have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So back in 1992, when this document was first seized in Sarajevo, who seized it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly who the person was who seized it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it seized pursuant to a search warrant?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: In discussions with members of the AID - and one of those was Mr. Alimanovic, but there were other people - one of the people we spoke to was familiar with the circumstances of the document having been seized. That person stated that in the spring of 1992, various SDS premises were searched by the AID. I do not know if it was in pursuance of a search warrant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why did these people go, whoever they were, go to find this document? Under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: After the start of the war, the information I have is that the SDS premises were vacant and therefore the premises were searched by the AID.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're talking about based on this information that you have, what information is it that you have? What is all the information regarding the seizure of this document?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The information is that the document was seized by AID staff in the spring of 1992 from SDS premises in Sarajevo. We also have details of the fact that the document was kept in the AID in Sarajevo. A copy -- a photocopy was provided. The first one was in 1994, then another in 1995, I believe, and then the original was taken by me in 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm trying -- "chain of custody" means from the date it was seized up until the date it comes into court. Who were all the persons who touched that document? That's what I'm trying to find out, Mr. O'Donnell, is this information that you have, we need to know, the Trial Chamber needs to know, the circumstances under which it was seized and from the date it was seized where that document has been. So who was the person who actually seized it? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I do not know. But if I could answer your questions, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know who the person is?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances under which that person, whoever it was, went to seize that document?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know exactly where that document was kept in this office in the SDS in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know if it was in a file drawer or if it was in a correspondence file or if it was in a propaganda file? You don't know where it was found at all. You have no information?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know who seized it in 1992, but based on this person giving it to you in 1997, you're assuming this document was kept where?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Do you mean before it was seized or after it being seized?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you took possession of it and brought it here to the ICTY, where was it kept?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It was kept in the offices of the AID in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in the offices of the AID?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: In a -- in various --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly requested to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Baen, can you please slow down and pause after the witness has answered, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours. I'm anxious to try to finish this today. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, within the AID were a number of cabinets. The cabinets were for the storage of information which came from various locations. The information that we were given in relation to this is that this document, after coming into the AID, was secured within the premises of the AID in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Employees of the AID in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the names of the employees?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: One of the people -- I've already stated, which is Mr. [redacted]. Another -- sorry, other employees, we would have to check. In relation to security concerns, Your Honours, I am aware that one does have security concerns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are the -- you mentioned in your statement that you had taken statements from all the people in the chain of custody with respect to PID 3. Where are those statements?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: We have statements from a number of people from the AID which are here within the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many statements are there?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I would have to check but at least three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why the Defence does not have these statements, have never been given copies of these statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a question which the witness is not in a position to answer. He's here to testify simply to the document and not to relationships between the Defence and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy. Ms. Baen? That is a submission you can make.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: The submission I'm making is we don't have any information with respect to the chain of custody of this document. They haven't given us anything. He says he's taken several statements. Who are they? What happened? How were these documents seized? Where was it kept? We have zero information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He's giving the answers as far as he knows. So if you're not satisfied with his answers, you can make your submissions on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He can't say what he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he took the statements himself, he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, he did say about three.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes. But he doesn't say what they say in the statements, he doesn't say the names, he doesn't give us the information that's in the statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I think Mr. O'Donnell has given the general information of the statements that -- where they were seized, when they were seized, where they were taken. He hasn't given the names for the reason put on the record, that there may be security concerns with individuals working for the AID and their role, particularly during the war and the seizure of documents. Maybe - I think to be fair to the witness - Ms. Baen would clarify what information she feels that is available to Mr. O'Donnell that he hasn't already provided that is contained in the statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Let me just try to shorten this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Baen, I'm just wondering, because the Prosecution sort of interjected and Ms. Reidy said that the issue of why the Defence doesn't have copies of those statements is a Defence-Prosecution issue, and this witness has, presumably, no control over the OTP sharing this information with you. So maybe that's an issue we might address, but not in the context of Mr. O'Donnell being able to assist on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, exactly. This is what I was asking. I was saying we could save a lot of time, maybe we wouldn't even be objecting to this document, if we had the information regarding the seizure of the document. That's the whole point. And that's why I -- if we could save the time by getting that from the Prosecution, if they want to redact the names of those witnesses or what have you, then that's fine. But to go on for hours and hours when we might not have to be doing this, is just -- I was trying to be reasonable. I really have been trying to be reasonable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Ms. Baen?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I'll just keep cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just one minute, please. In November last year, after the Court made certain rulings on these documents and requested that the Prosecution and the Defence cooperate on the matter, and you were given the summary and you -- or the other Defence lawyers saw these documents, was any request made from the Prosecution to provide the witness summaries? In other words, the persons who are concerned with these documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was no formal request. However, I've had numerous conversations with my colleague Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Did any Defence counsel put it in writing to the Prosecution, to end this matter, "Look, please let us have the statements of these witnesses so that we can have a look at them and make an informed decision?" Was that done?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, just very short explanation. In our, I would say, ongoing cooperation related to this particular issue, I cannot say precisely, but on many occasions, we asked from the Prosecution to provide us with all statements, documents, relevant issues, regarding the chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, that's all too general. What I meant is you've got a summary from the Prosecution, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And I think that summary must be saying certain things in respect of these documents, and also I don't know what it says but it may relate to tracing the history of these documents in some short way. Did you ask for amplification of this so you can decide then? And then we wouldn't have to waste this much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes, Your Honour. We -- I believe we work in bona fides manner and during all our conversation we asked every single detail in this respect. And finally, this is the first moment - I think that my colleagues would agree with me - that we realised that there are certain statements and number of statements. This is the first moment. Am I correct, Your Honours? For today, that we realise that there are several statements with regard to this issuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: But it must be quite obvious to everybody that this witness is not the one who seized the documents, that if they came from the AID office, they must have come down somehow through different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So that line was not pursued. That's all the I want to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see you, Judge Singh. It was pursued in that the purpose of this hearing, my understanding was, that he was -- this witness was going to give the whole chain of custody, the list of the witnesses, the circumstances under which they were seized, and then we didn't get it. That's -- my understanding in looking back at the transcript in this trial is that the purpose of this hearing was for the Prosecutors to prove up admissibility and authenticity, and it was -- I have mentioned to Ms. Reidy before, based on the witness summary they gave to us, that it doesn't have the whole chain of custody, but she told -- our conversation was that -- well, we had a difference in opinion as to what was required for the chain of custody apparently, even as recent as today in the hallway, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to me that the understanding of tracing from the origins of the seizure up to this witness's handling of the document seems to have been some misunderstanding. Since you are on your feet, you can go ahead with your cross-examination. I think to protect the names of the people who gave this document to the Office of the Prosecutor, we can have the witness write them down and then the document will be under seal, to complete the evidence of the witness, if you desire that, Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: The most important thing is not the names, it's the circumstances under which it was seized, because the whole test is reliability. And the case law in this Tribunal says also that we have the right to cross-examine the person who is sponsoring the witness who seized it or who authored it. The issue is not the names of the witness. The issue is the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe Ms. Baen could tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, since Mr. O'Donnell has said that there are at least three statements, what objection would you have to have those statements produced under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think there is -- well, there is two -- I would -- given that -- let me put it back. The production of these statements under seal would, in the normal course of things, protect the individuals' names from being allowed, permitted, to get into the public arena, and that I appreciate. There are, however, I am led to believe - I'm certainly not familiar with all these statements - a number of documents at any one time mentioned in these statements, not necessarily just Variant A/Variant B. I'm not sure it's clear that -- why Defence counsel need access to that sort of information. If that is the way the Trial Chamber wishes to proceed, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. You were explaining that these statements are not only dealing with the documents at issue in this case. They are statements dealing with a whole variety of documents, in which case maybe the larger part of the statement may not be relevant. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: If that is the -- if the Trial Chamber wishes to direct that we should disclose chain of custody statements taken, then I would -- well, request, if that's the ruling of the Trial Chamber, that we would be able to redact bits of the statements which have no relevancy to this document trial and with -- preferably redact the names, since Ms. Baen has indicated it's not of any interest to her, as to the name of the person who actually seized the document. However, I would submit, of course, we will comply with any order that the Trial Chamber would hand down. But again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Have you seen the statements yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The exact three Mr. O'Donnell is referring to, I'm honestly not sure, but yes, I have seen a number of statements which relate to chain of custody of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's stick to the ones Mr. O'Donnell has mentioned, about three statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: There is a statement at paragraph 4 of his witness summary, which again I'm not sure if the bench have copies of this. And it says that the witness took a statement from an employee regarding chain of custody, stating that the document was found in the main office of the Sarajevo SDS party. That document -- that statement I can tell the Chamber I definitely -- I have read. And I have read a number of other chain of custody statements. I'm not sure I've read all the ones relating to this document but certainly a number of statements which have been taken relating to chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because you see, if you read the three referred to by Mr. O'Donnell and if you're in a position to redact them and leave only the relevant information and redact the names as well, maybe that can be done. That would satisfy the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, if it's the Trial Chamber's instructions, then we would make available the statements redacted of any information not relating to any other document and of specific names of employees of the AID, but I would again ask for these statements to be kept under seal by the Defence because they are someone's internal -- I know they do relate somehow to admissibility, but they are also internal OTP documents that somebody from our records -- and again I do believe that with respect to the rules of evidence on admissibility, they are primarily governed by Rule 89, as a rule, the general disclosure of these statements are not -- is not required, notwithstanding Ms. Baen's submissions on admissibility. But as I said, we would -- I can locate those statements, I can have them redacted leaving the information relevant to Variant A and Variant B open to the Defence, and again, redact statements of particular -- specific employees who may be endangered by their name getting into the public sphere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe what we can do is we will give you the time after tomorrow, you look at the statements and then make your submissions as you see fit. Maybe because you read so many of them so you can't really be clear in your mind which ones are -- Mr. O'Donnell was talking about when he mentioned about three.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I said the one reference in paragraph 4 of Mr. O'Donnell's, I -- definitely, I can tell the Chamber now, would require specific redactions, including the name of the employee, and I will undertake to investigate more closely the other statements. Do I understand, then, from Your Honour that when you say, "Make your submissions," you would mean, "Make your submissions on the disclosure of these statements," or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Finally, finally, at the end of the day. Yes, Ms. Baen, you can go ahead, if you have any more questions, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I do have more questions, but without the statement and the people -- how can I cross-examine if I don't have the information on chain of custody? I'm not clear. If the Chamber could give me some guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought the witness had given you some answers of the matters which he knew about and of the matters which he didn't know about. Are you saying that of the matters which he doesn't know about, because of that, you have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Well, he could not give me the answer as to the entire chain of custody from 1992 to 1997, and that's the whole issue. So that's why -- he said there were three witness statements taken, but I have no idea what the witness statement said, and he doesn't have the statements here. So there is nothing to cross-examine him on until I have the information to cross-examine him on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I'll go into another area to try to move things forward but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is what I was trying to get at, any other area while we wait for the statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about your knowledge of -- your general knowledge of documents created in Bosnia and the former Yugoslavia. As an investigator for the OTP, and a team leader, you've seen and handled probably thousands of documents right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many from Bosnia and all of the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at ID 3, there is no stamp or seal on that document, is there?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is no signature, is there?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it looks sort of like it could be a draft and not an official document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think now Ms. Baen is asking the witness, you know, opinion, and then she is making assumptions about what a draft looks like. I mean, it is obvious that it doesn't have a seal and it doesn't a signature. What that means is not -- Mr. Donia could have testified to this but the Defence wouldn't allow him. I think it's unfair now to ask the witness who has come to testify to the admissibility of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, he can't be asked what about what his opinion of it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought he had handled lots of -- reviewed lots of documents. And with respect to Dr. Donia, he did testify about this very thing. I have the transcript right here in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can recall some of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Authenticity, whether or not there was a stamp, a seal or a signature, according to, again, the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, goes to authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Baen, I understand asking was there a stamp, was there a signature and so on, but correct me if I'm wrong here, but I thought in your opening with this witness in your cross-examination, you reminded the Chamber that Mr. O'Donnell is not an expert on authenticating documents. So now, this seems to be at cross-purposes with your initial submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I see your point. I see your point, Judge -- Your Honour. Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the documents you reviewed in your investigations, the documents from Serbia, the -- or and Bosnia-Herzegovina, the official documents usually have a stamp or a seal or a signature; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you testified that this document has none of those on it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the name Bosanski Samac anywhere on ID 3?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any evidence that ID 3 was ever distributed in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No there is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anyone who can testify what the -- who the number 100 refers to specifically?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, there is not, that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to these other versions of the A/B document that you've brought up. But before I go into those different versions, when you were testifying about them, you mentioned Bosanski Petrovac and Bosanska Krupa; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Bosanska Krupa and Bosanski Petrovac, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And neither Bosanska Krupa or Bosanski Petrovac are anywhere near Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it's in western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the different documents you talked about, before we -- excuse me, before we go into the different versions of the A/B document, let's talk about the transcripts from the speeches and these various minutes from the different municipalities you discussed. Let's focus first on the speech transcripts. In these speech transcripts that you read to the Chamber and have reviewed, was the Variant A/B document ever read out in totality in those speech transcripts?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: One of the documents refers to -- and I'm not sure whether it was the whole of the document being read out or part of it so I'm just checking that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it appears to have been. The Prijedor municipal board of the SDS minutes from the 27th of December, 1991, it appears that the document was read out there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document was read out in totality?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It says, "President Miskovic then read out the instructions forwarded," and it is apparently referring to this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says he read an entire document, but they don't read out the entire document, so we have no idea exactly what that document said; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It is correct that the document -- sorry, the reading of the document is not recorded in the minutes. However, as to whether we know what was said, the details given indicate the substance of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can we know what the substance was if we don't have the minutes and we don't have a transcript wherein all of the document was read?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, four things that I can point to in those minutes: Firstly, the establishment of the assembly; secondly, the establishment of Crisis Staffs; thirdly, introducing around-the-clock duty in SDS offices; and fourthly, the composition of the Crisis Staff, which appear to be in line with what was in that document. So even though it's not read out -- sorry, it's not recorded what was actually said when it was read out, what was discussed refers to the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If -- maybe conceptually, it could have been the same as this PID 3. However, there is no way to know what the actual content was unless it was read out, correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I would disagree because of the points I've just made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anywhere in that transcript, was there any information with respect to who the author of this Variant A/B document is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me Ms. Baen, when you're saying, "the transcript," we are talking about the last document in this bundle, the -- are we? Because otherwise we will have a confusion between the use of the words "abridged minutes" and "transcript."

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- in P46 ID, I was referring to the transcript of the speech given by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, but as with the Prosecution, if you can give us the numbers, then there will be no confusion on the record either. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to the -- who the author of this Variant A/B document is?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm going to have to interrupt and seek a ruling from the Chamber as to whether or not this question is relevant. I know Ms. Baen says that she wants to establish who the author is and she feels it goes to admissibility, but the Rules - and I'm afraid these are legal submissions - say that any evidence may be admitted which has probative value and the evidence -- and the Chamber may call evidence as to authenticity. Nowhere in the Rules or in the jurisprudence is it said that evidence can only be admitted where authenticity -- or where authorship is established. So why Ms. Baen -- again, I just think that this is an irrelevant line of questioning because it doesn't go to the Rules of Evidence applicable in this Tribunal, which is whether or not this document has -- is of probative value.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I can read directly from case law here in the jurisprudence. It's from Prosecutor versus Aleksovski where the Appeals Chamber said -- and the judgement Aleksovski -- excuse me, in Celebici and Tadic says, it's Prosecutor versus Delalic decision on the motion of the Prosecution for the admissibility [microphone not activated] 1998, the Chamber in that case, relying on the Tadic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Baen, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: The Chamber in the above -- in this case, relying on the Tadic hearsay decision, held that in assessing the probative value --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You're not slowing down, Ms. Baen. You are too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll try to slow down. I just want to get this over with. "An important factor would be whether or not the alleged author of the document appears as a witness. Otherwise, the contents of a document remain unauthenticated and not subject to the kind of scrutiny which comes with the cross-examination of the witness." The Chamber in another decision, Prosecutor versus Delalic judgement, November 16, 1998, the Chamber found the documents, although may be relevant to the issue at hand, none of them have been authenticated as the parties alleged to have created them never gave evidence. The Chamber said that because there was no evidence of authenticity, they were unreliable and attached no weight to them. And then I can keep citing more case law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. It's not necessary because that's what I said earlier, that these are matters for submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I was answering Ms. Reidy's response saying that nowhere in the jurisprudence was there a requirement that the author testify in order to authenticate a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think you can go ahead with your cross-examination. I think both parties seem to be confusing what they should make in their submissions and what should be put out in cross-examination. I think they are having a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'll try to get through this. I'm just answering Ms. Reidy's submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Ms. Baen, what do you mean by "who is the author"? The document here at the top says -- or claims to say that is the main board. Maybe there are ten authors, I don't know, five authors, three authors. You follow?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I do follow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: That's what it says there: " Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, main board." And it does appear, for what it's worth at the moment, that the main board issued this document, that it may have been the author of this document. So when you talk about authorship, can you call, say, 10 people, 15 people? You won't know who they are, who made the drafts, who finally -- it is a whole process. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I do follow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: This is an important document or seems to be an important document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I think it's the most important document in this trial so far, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: The document says -- or purports to have been authored by a group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: There has been no testimony that someone authored that. We have no evidence so far as to who wrote the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: No. Direct your questions to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was going to continue. My counsel just said to remind the Chamber it's 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe you can complete your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I have a bunch more questions, Your Honours. And the most important part would be the chain of custody with respect to the document PID 3 between 1992 and 1997. And if we could review those statements, maybe I won't have any questions, which -- I would love it if I had no questions. I don't want to talk about this any more, really. And I know you don't want to hear about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's up to you, Ms. Baen. What I can say is that the Prosecution should produce those statements redacted to the Defence before 11.00 tomorrow morning. Do not wait for the sitting time, because we don't want to waste any more trial time. We have the whole morning tomorrow to deal with this, so that the Defence can look at those documents so that when we start our proceedings at 14.15, we'll be in a position -- they'll be in a position to say whether or not they'll proceed with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Absolutely. No problem with complying with that time line. And if the Defence wants to come to the Tribunal earlier, we can probably make the documents available earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Trial Chamber will order the Defence counsels to be at the Tribunal by 10 hours. And by then, the Prosecution must be ready with the documents. So at least before 11 hours give it to them so that there is time to look at them, consult with each other, consult with their clients, and then be able to inform the Prosecution or be ready for the proceedings at 14.15. We have to use the mornings, even though we are not sitting, for everything that has to be done in the cases, in the ongoing trials, instead of waiting for trial time to start discussing what should have been discussed outside trial time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. And I'm happy to use this evening and tomorrow out of court time to satisfy the requests of the Defence. But I would ask that they place on the record or in writing exactly what it is they're looking for, because -- I think Chamber is probably apprised of the fact there's been a misunderstanding of this. Is it simply document copy 100 or is it another chain of custody statements with relation to, for example, number 96 from Trnovo, which Mr. O'Donnell has testified to, or are we referring only to those statements which specifically and explicitly record some handling of the Variant A/Variant B with copy number "100" in the corner? Now, if that could be clarified preferably on the record with some written record I can keep going back to, that would be of great assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Very clearly, as we pointed out last fall, we're only interested in PID 3, the document that has the number "100" on it. We do not care anything about the chain of custody on any of these other versions of A/B. We don't care about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think that is clear. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just one other matter that might arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: The original, I see, is just behind the law clerks. I don't know if you want to look at it. May I suggest that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we may go ahead and look at it now, now that we have adjourned the proceedings formally. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If Your Honours, please, the witness is in fact the expert on all the sorts of procedures that I think must be undertaken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it would be better if the witness can unseal it, handle it. We don't only have to view it. We don't have to handle it. MR. DI FAZIO: I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. Maybe we can proceed with that now. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I think that could be adopted to maybe maintain its integrity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe the document could be given to Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I should have got fitted up for those gloves beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Go ahead, and we'll wait patiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. In the meantime, maybe we should have certain technical problems tomorrow morning in light of the beginning of the trial -- the big trial tomorrow. So maybe the security will not allow us to come to the Tribunal and -- or maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I doubt that very much, because all the lawyers and supporting staff who have continuing trials are allowed into the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. It's better. Because maybe certain level of assistance from the Registry could be useful to inform the guards at the entrance that we have certain things to do here. Because I don't know really how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. Because the proceedings which are going on tomorrow will continue, and so the Defence counsel can -- will be allowed into the Tribunal any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document is unsealed. Would you like me to put that on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Can you walk with it, you know, let us view it, and show it to the Defence counsel. It doesn't have to be on the ELMO. Yes, you can just hold it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It was seen already, wasn't it, by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, apart from the handwritten "100," what is the "26" in the circle, centre top of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what that number refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: If you would look at the number "100," and if you would also compare it with the others that you have talked about today, I would like you to study the print and just tell me whether "100" is a photocopy, whether it's a print copy, or a typed copy. You can do that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Did you want me to tell you whether the -- where it is written in, 100, whether that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: No, no. The content. The content. Just have a look at it carefully and just give us your opinion, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. The proceedings will continue tomorrow at 14.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Just for the record, although Mr. O'Donnell has taken the oath and is currently under cross-examination, I presume for the purpose of production of these documents that I'm allowed to talk to him and discuss the documents and the location of them and redaction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of the statements, yes. I'm sure the Defence would have no objection, so that we have the matter dealt with in the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: No objection at all, whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would like the witness to leave the courtroom. Perhaps he can take the document with him, since he has to look at it. I just want to discuss a few matters before we rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The arrangements for the videolink from the Detention Unit into the courtroom has been finalised by the Registrar's Office. We have been informed that it is possible for Mr. Milan Simic if he's in the Detention Unit to follow the proceedings. He can view us -- he can view the courtroom. He can also communicate with counsel by phone. But we cannot have it the other way; we can't see him, which is really not necessary. So I wanted to advise the Defence counsel for Milan Simic to look at these facilities and see how best we can utilise them. As indicated earlier, when we were requesting for these facilities, the Trial Chamber is interested in sitting longer hours in order to get on with the trial, because we've been handicapped by the health of Mr. Milan Simic. So these facilities are available, and I do expect that the Defence counsel will discuss with their client. We'll look at the proceedings as they go. We'll see whether or not the facilities will enable him to follow and be able to communicate, so that with the three remaining accused persons, we can perhaps take advantage of the longer sitting hours, even if it's for half day, and move much faster that we are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We understand, Your Honours, and that is exactly what we intended to do tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So we will rise now and continue our proceedings tomorrow at 14.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
